paragraphs: AGILE treats a conversational agent as a system that learns how to act while answering questions. Its language model can draw on memory, use tools, reflect on its progress, and consult experts. The central problem is therefore broader than generating an answer: the agent must also decide which supporting actions will help.

The framework expresses these decisions as a reinforcement learning problem, with the language model serving as the policy that selects actions. Training uses labeled action data and the PPO reinforcement learning algorithm. This connects the model’s conversational abilities to learning how to use the resources available in its environment.

The authors introduce ProductQA, a dataset of challenging online shopping questions, and evaluate on it alongside MedMCQA and HotPotQA. In these experiments, PPO-trained agents using 7B and 13B models can outperform GPT-4 agents. Ablation experiments identify memory, tools, consultation, reflection, and reinforcement learning as essential contributors to the reported performance. The findings emphasize the importance of training the agent’s behavior as well as choosing its underlying language model.
neurips-2024-agile-a-novel-reinforcement.tldr: AGILE trains language models to coordinate memory, tools, reflection, and expert consultation through reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: This paper studies predictions involving three biological entities, such as a drug, a target protein, and an adverse reaction. Such relationships matter for understanding drug effects. The authors argue that existing methods concentrate on collecting information around individual entities while overlooking patterns in how different entities are associated.

Their method brings those association patterns directly into the process of learning entity representations. This gives the model information about relationships alongside information about the entities themselves. A separate bind-relation module accounts for strongly connected lower-order associations, addressing information that the authors say ordinary lower-order message passing misses.

Experiments on three biological datasets report approximately 4%–23% improvements in hit@1 over state-of-the-art baselines. This metric concerns whether the correct prediction occupies the highest-ranked position, making the result relevant to prioritizing candidate relationships. The paper also examines how association patterns can be interpreted in biological terms. Together, these findings support using relationship patterns as explicit predictive information and as a way to explain the model’s biological predictions.
neurips-2024-association-pattern-aware-f.tldr: Explicitly modeling biological association patterns improves predictions involving triples of entities and supports interpretation of those predictions.

paragraphs: BackdoorAlign addresses a safety problem in services that let users fine-tune language models. A small number of harmful examples in uploaded training data can undermine a model’s existing safety behavior. Adding ordinary safety examples can help, but the paper identifies the large amount of additional data required as an efficiency problem.

The proposed defense trains an association between a secret prompt prefix and safe responses. The service provider adds that prefix to safety examples included during fine-tuning. At inference time, the provider prepends the same secret prompt to user inputs, activating the learned safety behavior. The method borrows the trigger mechanism associated with backdoor attacks and uses it for defensive alignment.

In the reported experiments, adding as few as 11 prefixed safety examples brings maliciously fine-tuned models to safety performance similar to the original aligned models, without harming benign performance. The authors also evaluate mixtures of attack examples and legitimate task data. These results support the defense in the tested service setting, where the provider controls both the added safety examples and the inference-time prefix.
neurips-2024-backdooralign-mitigating-fi.tldr: BackdoorAlign associates a secret prompt prefix with safe responses to counter safety degradation from malicious fine-tuning.

paragraphs: This paper investigates reducing the cost of transformer language models by restructuring their feedforward networks. These components consume substantial computation but have received less attention than attention blocks. The authors study three ways to represent their linear transformations using low-rank and block-diagonal matrices, which impose structure on otherwise dense parameter matrices.

The study trains these models from scratch and scales experiments to 1.3 billion parameters. Structured layers can have poor training dynamics when introduced at initialization, so the authors propose self-guided training to improve that process. They also demonstrate computational gains in several settings, including online decoding with a technique called pre-merge.

The scaling results suggest that these structures become more attractive as training computation increases, including in the overtraining regime. In the reported comparisons, wide structured networks can achieve lower loss with fewer parameters while using training FLOPs more efficiently than dense models at their optimal trade-off. The contribution therefore combines an efficient architecture with a training strategy that helps realize its potential.
neurips-2024-building-on-efficient-found.tldr: Structured feedforward layers and self-guided training can improve language models’ parameter and computation efficiency when trained from scratch.

paragraphs: COLD evaluates whether language models understand causal relationships in familiar daily activities. The paper identifies a gap between two existing approaches: everyday commonsense questions provide real-world grounding but can lack formal validation, while symbolic causal questions support theoretical analysis but can feel disconnected from ordinary activities.

The framework builds on human understanding of daily tasks to connect grounded events with causal reasoning. It supports generating approximately nine million causal queries, providing a large collection of questions about how events relate within these activities. The authors position this as an approximation to a small test of humanlike understanding of a daily task.

Evaluations across multiple language models find that causal reasoning remains difficult even when the underlying activities seem trivial to humans. The paper also explores models’ causal reasoning using the backdoor criterion to determine causal strength between events. Its contribution is both a framework for constructing grounded causal evaluations and evidence that familiarity with everyday subject matter does not by itself establish reliable causal understanding.
neurips-2024-cold-causal-reasoning-in-cl.tldr: COLD generates large-scale causal questions about daily activities and finds that they challenge multiple language models.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how feedback could help recurrent neural circuits determine which activity changes will reduce errors. The biological motivation is that brain circuits contain extensive recurrence and feedback, while the way these connections support local synaptic learning remains unclear. The study examines pretrained recurrent networks with feedback control on a standard motor task.

The authors show that feedback adjustments to ongoing network activity approximate the optimal first-order gradient with respect to that activity. This allows movement corrections while a movement is underway. They also examine learning across repeated trials under a persistent perturbation, using a local learning rule that combines recent activity with error feedback.

With feedback control during learning, this trial-by-trial adaptation becomes more accurate and efficient. The authors attribute the improvement to decoupling recurrent dynamics and introducing an adaptive second-order gradient into those dynamics. These modeled results suggest a possible mechanism through which feedback supports both immediate correction and longer-term learning. The biological conclusion remains a proposed explanation of credit assignment, grounded in the studied network behavior.
neurips-2024-feedback-control-guides-cre.tldr: Feedback control can guide activity corrections and improve local learning in recurrent networks, suggesting a mechanism for biological credit assignment.

paragraphs: FindingEmo is a dataset for studying emotion recognition in complex social images. It contains annotations for 25,000 images and focuses on naturalistic settings with multiple people. The main contribution is the choice of what receives an emotion annotation: each image is judged as a whole, extending beyond the familiar focus on individual faces or single people.

The annotations cover three dimensions: valence, arousal, and an emotion label. Valence describes the positive or negative character of an emotional impression, while arousal describes its level of activation. Including these dimensions alongside a categorical label provides several ways to describe the emotional character assigned to an entire scene.

Annotations were gathered through Prolific. The release includes those annotations, URLs pointing to the original images, and the associated source code. This makes the dataset a resource for research that treats emotion recognition as a scene-level task. Its distinctive emphasis is on the overall emotional impression of multi-person social settings, rather than assigning a separate emotional judgment to each depicted individual.
neurips-2024-findingemo-an-image-dataset.tldr: FindingEmo provides whole-image emotion annotations for 25,000 images featuring complex, naturalistic social scenes.

paragraphs: GGAD studies anomaly detection in graphs where some nodes are known to be normal. This differs from detecting anomalies in a completely unlabeled graph. The authors first show that even a small proportion of labeled normal nodes can improve existing unsupervised methods when those methods are adapted to use this information.

Their proposed approach makes more use of the normal examples by generating artificial outlier nodes. These become negative training examples for a discriminative one-class classifier. Because real anomalies have no ground-truth labels in this setting, the generator relies on two priors, asymmetric local affinity and egocentric closeness, to produce outliers that resemble anomalies in both graph structure and node features.

Experiments on six real-world datasets establish a benchmark for this semi-supervised setting. GGAD substantially outperforms the compared unsupervised and semi-supervised methods across different quantities of labeled normal nodes. The findings support the idea that normal examples can help define useful synthetic counterexamples, giving the classifier a stronger training signal despite the absence of labeled real anomalies.
neurips-2024-generative-semi-supervised-.tldr: GGAD uses known normal graph nodes and anomaly priors to generate synthetic outliers that improve anomaly detection.

paragraphs: HairDiffusion edits hairstyle and hair color from text descriptions or reference images while aiming to preserve unrelated attributes. Multi-colored hair creates a particular challenge because an editor must control where colors appear as well as the shape of the hair. The paper identifies spatial limitations in existing StyleGAN-based approaches that affect both multi-color editing and facial preservation.

The method uses latent diffusion models and introduces Multi-stage Hairstyle Blend to separate control of color and hairstyle within the diffusion representation. A trained warping module aligns hair color with the intended target region. The authors also fine-tune a CLIP model on a multi-color hairstyle dataset to support the more demanding color-editing task.

These components address both the placement of multiple colors and the preservation of original colors during diffusion editing. The reported experiments show superior multi-color hairstyle editing while maintaining facial attributes, using either textual descriptions or reference images. The central contribution is coordinated control over hairstyle, color, and spatial alignment within an editing system.
neurips-2024-hairdiffusion-vivid-multi-c.tldr: HairDiffusion separates hairstyle and color control in latent diffusion to improve multi-colored hair editing while preserving facial attributes.

paragraphs: HORSE addresses selecting a useful subset from a large collection, a problem that appears in anomaly detection and compound selection for drug discovery. Neural set models account for the fact that reordering a collection should not change its meaning. However, the paper argues that existing architectures can miss information about the full collection or complex interactions among its elements.

The authors introduce an Identity Property requiring models to incorporate information from the set that a subset comes from. Their attention-based HORSE method learns interactions while retaining information from both the input collection and supervision specifying the optimal subset. This connects decisions about selected elements to the broader set containing them.

HORSE also supports dividing a collection into chunks that can be processed independently and then combined, with consistent results across different partitions. This addresses inputs larger than available memory. Experiments report improved subset selection and gains of up to 20% over state-of-the-art methods for large inputs, supporting the combination of richer set representations and manageable chunk-based processing.
neurips-2024-horse-hierarchical-represen.tldr: HORSE improves large-scale subset selection by preserving whole-set information while allowing consistent processing in manageable chunks.

paragraphs: IRCAN addresses situations where a language model’s stored knowledge conflicts with information supplied in its current context. For example, knowledge encoded during training may be outdated or incorrect. The paper focuses on helping generation respond to the new contextual information when that conflict arises.

The framework first identifies neurons that contribute strongly to processing context. It does this with a context-aware attribution score derived from integrated gradients, a method for attributing contributions within a model. IRCAN then strengthens the identified neurons through reweighting, increasing the influence of components already involved in using contextual cues.

This approach aims to steer outputs toward the supplied knowledge by modifying how strongly context-processing neurons contribute. Experiments across multiple models and tasks report substantial improvements in handling knowledge conflicts. The authors also describe IRCAN as scalable and easy to integrate with existing models. The findings support targeted adjustment of internal context processing as a practical way to improve context-sensitive generation when stored and supplied knowledge disagree.
neurips-2024-ircan-mitigating-knowledge-.tldr: IRCAN identifies and strengthens context-processing neurons to help language models resolve conflicts between stored knowledge and supplied information.

paragraphs: LAM3D reconstructs a three-dimensional mesh from a single image. The paper targets geometric inaccuracies that arise when reconstruction models must infer shape from image information alone. Its approach uses three-dimensional point clouds to develop a stronger geometric representation that can subsequently guide reconstruction from an image.

The first component is a point-cloud network that produces latent tri-planes, an internal representation used for mesh reconstruction. The second component aligns features from a single image with those point-cloud-derived representations. Through this alignment, image features gain access to information about three-dimensional structure, helping the reconstruction process retain more accurate geometry.

The resulting system does not require multiple input views when reconstructing a mesh. The authors report reduced geometric distortions, state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity, and a reconstruction time of six seconds, with effectiveness demonstrated on several datasets. The central idea is to transfer geometric information from point-cloud representations into image processing, making a single image a more useful starting point for producing a detailed three-dimensional mesh.
neurips-2024-lam3d-large-image-point-clo.tldr: LAM3D aligns image features with point-cloud-derived representations to reconstruct more accurate 3D meshes from a single image.

paragraphs: This paper seeks a precise probabilistic interpretation of deep neural networks. Probabilistic graphical models explicitly describe relationships between random variables, giving their computations a defined probabilistic meaning. The authors aim to connect neural-network computation to that kind of interpretation by constructing corresponding graphical models.

Their construction uses infinite tree-structured probabilistic graphical models that correspond exactly to neural networks. It explains forward propagation through the lens of inference: computations viewed as approximations to graphical-model inference become precise in the alternative structure they construct. The distinction matters because the exact correspondence concerns this particular infinite-tree representation.

The result adds another perspective alongside interpretations of neural networks as kernel machines or infinite Gaussian processes. Its contribution is a more direct account of the approximation neural networks make relative to exact probabilistic inference. The authors identify improved teaching, clearer interpretation, and algorithms combining graphical models with neural networks as potential benefits. These are possibilities enabled by the theoretical connection, rather than reported demonstrations of improved application performance.
neurips-2024-on-neural-networks-as-infin.tldr: The paper constructs infinite tree-structured graphical models that give neural-network forward propagation a precise probabilistic interpretation.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization problems whose variables are multiple probability distributions, as occurs in policy optimization. It introduces generalized quasar-convexity, a condition extending beyond ordinary convexity. Each block of variables receives its own parameter describing its degree of block-convexity, allowing different parts of the problem to have different optimization geometry.

The authors develop optimistic mirror descent using a generalized information source that includes ordinary gradients as a special case. For objectives with the stated polynomial-like structure, they prove an adaptive iteration bound proportional, up to suppressed factors, to the sum of inverse block parameters divided by the target error. The algorithm does not need those parameters in advance.

This bound uses the individual block parameters instead of multiplying the worst inverse parameter by the number of blocks, giving the stated improvement over mirror descent. The authors also extend the condition to minimax problems and propose a decentralized regularized algorithm. Applications to discounted Markov decision processes and Markov games connect the framework to understanding optimization landscapes in reinforcement learning.
neurips-2024-optimizing-over-multiple-di.tldr: Generalized quasar-convexity enables adaptive optimization guarantees that account for the differing geometry of multiple probability distributions.

paragraphs: PV-Tuning studies language-model compression to just one or two bits per parameter. Such compression supports execution on resource-constrained devices, but preserving accuracy becomes difficult. The paper focuses on fine-tuning compressed weights, motivated by diminishing gains from methods that only quantize a model after training.

Existing approaches often use straight-through estimators to train through compressed representations. The authors show that this strategy can be suboptimal and systematically examine alternatives for quantization-aware fine-tuning. Their proposed PV-Tuning framework generalizes and improves existing strategies without depending on a particular weight representation. It also supplies convergence guarantees in restricted cases.

For one- and two-bit vector quantization, experiments report better results than prior techniques on Llama and Mistral models. The authors further report the first Pareto-optimal two-bit quantization for the Llama-2 family, addressing the balance between accuracy and compression. The findings make fine-tuning strategy a central part of extreme compression: how compressed parameters are optimized can matter alongside the representation used to store them.
neurips-2024-pv-tuning-beyond-straight-t.tldr: PV-Tuning improves fine-tuning of extremely compressed language models beyond conventional straight-through estimation.

paragraphs: Segment, Shuffle, and Stitch asks whether the original temporal order is always the best arrangement for learning from a time series. Distant parts of a sequence can have strong dependencies. The proposed S3 layer lets a model learn an alternative arrangement that may make those relationships easier to use for the task.

S3 divides the sequence into non-overlapping segments, learns how to reorder them, and joins them into a new sequence. It then combines this rearranged sequence with the original using a learned weighted sum. The model therefore retains access to the original ordering while also using the learned arrangement. Multiple layers can be stacked to operate at different levels of granularity.

The layer can be added to architectures including convolutional networks and transformers with negligible reported computational overhead. Experiments cover classification, forecasting, and anomaly detection, with improvements reaching 68% on certain datasets. The authors also report smoother training loss curves and loss landscapes, indicating more stable learning in the evaluated comparisons.
neurips-2024-segment-shuffle-and-stitch-.tldr: S3 learns to rearrange time-series segments and blend them with the original sequence to improve representations and training stability.

paragraphs: SLED aims to improve the factual accuracy of language-model outputs during decoding, the process that selects generated text. It uses knowledge already present within the model and requires neither an external knowledge base nor additional fine-tuning. The central question is how to make better use of information expressed at different model depths.

The method compares output logits, or token scores, from early layers with those from the final layer. It interprets their differences through an optimization perspective and uses an approximate gradient to guide output refinement. This gives intermediate model information a role in shaping the final generated response.

Experiments span LLaMA 2, LLaMA 3, and Gemma models from 2B to 70B parameters, as well as mixture-of-experts configurations. Evaluations include multiple-choice questions, open generation, and adaptations for chain-of-thought reasoning. The authors report consistent factuality gains reaching 20% over existing decoding methods, while retaining fluency and adding negligible latency. They also find that SLED can combine with other decoding approaches for further improvements.
neurips-2024-sled-self-logits-evolution-.tldr: SLED compares token scores across model layers to improve factual generation without additional training or external knowledge.

paragraphs: This paper tackles compressive sensing: recovering a signal from compressed linear measurements. It introduces a generative prior that combines a preference for sparse solutions with the ability to adapt to training data. The motivation is to bring together the structural guidance of classical sparse reconstruction and the flexibility of learned generative models.

The method draws on dictionary-based compressive sensing and sparse Bayesian learning to encourage sparsity. Conditional Gaussian structure supplies the connection to a data-adaptive generative model. The resulting approach can learn from a small number of compressed, noisy samples and does not require an optimization algorithm to solve the inverse problem.

The model also parameterizes a conjugate prior, enabling uncertainty quantification alongside reconstruction. The authors support the construction theoretically using variational inference and evaluate it on different types of compressible signals. Its contribution is therefore a combined treatment of sparse reconstruction, learning from limited measurements, and uncertainty, with empirical validation across the signal types studied.
neurips-2024-sparse-bayesian-generative-.tldr: A sparse Bayesian generative prior learns from limited noisy compressed data and supports reconstruction with uncertainty quantification.

paragraphs: Star-Agents automates the improvement of instruction-tuning datasets. These datasets strongly influence how language models perform on downstream tasks, but collecting varied, high-quality examples is expensive. The framework uses multiple language-model agents to generate and assess instruction data, making dataset refinement an explicit collaborative process.

Its workflow has three parts. First, a specialized sampling method draws on multiple agents to produce diverse instructions. Second, a dual-model assessment evaluates the generated data for both difficulty and quality. Third, a dynamic refinement stage gives greater priority to models that prove more effective, adjusting the process as it proceeds.

Instruction-tuning experiments include Pythia and LLaMA models, with evaluation using MT-bench, Vicuna bench, and the WizardLM test set. The authors report an average improvement of 12% and a 40% improvement on Fermi. These findings support the value of jointly managing generation, evaluation, and model selection when improving training data. The reported gains concern models trained with the optimized datasets, linking the data workflow to downstream performance.
neurips-2024-star-agents-automatic-data-.tldr: Star-Agents uses collaborative generation, dual-model assessment, and adaptive refinement to improve instruction-tuning data.

paragraphs: TARSS-Net improves radar semantic segmentation, which aims to extract fine-grained information about targets from radar data. The paper focuses on temporal information: observations from different times can help interpret a target, but the authors argue that existing segmentation frameworks do not use this information sufficiently.

The proposed approach learns relationships between a target and its history, then uses those relationships to combine temporal information. Its central component, the Temporal Relation-Aware Module, contains an encoder for target-history relationships and a learnable attentive pooling block. The encoder represents temporal connections, while the pooling block uses learned relations when aggregating information.

The authors incorporate this module into an end-to-end radar segmentation network. They report strong performance on publicly available datasets and on real measured data they collected. The contribution is a data-driven way to connect temporal relationship learning with information aggregation inside the segmentation model. This makes the treatment of a target’s history an explicit part of how the network interprets radar observations.
neurips-2024-tarss-net-temporal-aware-ra.tldr: TARSS-Net learns target-history relationships to aggregate temporal information for radar semantic segmentation.

paragraphs: TaskBench evaluates how well language models turn user instructions into tasks that external tools can execute. This involves several distinct abilities, so a single overall judgment can obscure where a model succeeds or struggles. The benchmark organizes automation into task decomposition, tool selection, and parameter prediction.

The framework represents decomposed tasks using a Tool Graph and employs a back-instruct method to generate user instructions. Its TaskEval methodology evaluates performance across all three stages. Automated benchmark construction is combined with human verification, and the authors report high consistency with human evaluation.

Experiments show that TaskBench reflects differences in automation capabilities across language models, task complexities, and domains. Separating the stages helps make those differences interpretable: organizing the work, choosing an appropriate tool, and supplying its inputs are evaluated as distinct parts of automation. The paper’s contribution is a scalable and adaptable evaluation framework for autonomous agents, providing a more systematic basis for assessing how models translate requests into executable plans.
neurips-2024-taskbench-benchmarking-larg.tldr: TaskBench evaluates language-model automation through task decomposition, tool selection, and parameter prediction.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether the shape of a model’s training trajectory can help explain generalization. Previous topology-based approaches use properties such as fractal dimension, often assuming continuous-time or infinite-time training dynamics. Those assumptions complicate practical estimation from the finite sequence of updates produced by actual training.

The authors instead work directly with discrete-time trajectories. They develop topological complexity measures suited to topological data analysis and prove that these measures bound generalization error without the restrictive geometric assumptions used previously. Computationally efficient procedures turn the theoretical quantities into practical generalization indices.

Experiments find strong correlations between the proposed measures and generalization error across architectures including transformers and deep graph networks. The approach also outperforms existing topological bounds across the evaluated datasets, models, and optimizers. The contribution connects a theoretical account of trajectory complexity with quantities that can be computed from realistic training runs, supporting their use in assessing generalization without requiring test data for the index itself.
neurips-2024-topological-generalization-.tldr: Topology-based measures of discrete training trajectories provide computable generalization bounds and correlate strongly with observed generalization error.

paragraphs: This paper examines how AI explanations influence people who use AI recommendations to make decisions. Explanations are often intended to help people decide when to trust an automated recommendation. The authors ask whether modeling that decision process can also enable explanations to be altered in ways that steer people toward a chosen outcome.

The approach quantitatively models how people combine recommendations and explanations when making their final decisions. The learned behavioral understanding is then used to manipulate the explanations. The study considers both benign and adversarial intentions, examining whether the same ability to predict human responses can support either kind of influence.

Human experiments across several tasks show that these manipulated explanations can readily shift decisions toward targeted outcomes. Participants often do not notice anomalies in the explanations even when their choices are affected. The findings identify a tension in explanation design: understanding how explanations help users can also reveal how to steer them. An explanation’s influence and its apparent acceptability therefore need to be understood together.
neurips-2024-utilizing-human-behavior-mo.tldr: Learned models of human decision-making can guide explanation changes that influence users, often without users noticing.

paragraphs: Weak-to-Strong Search uses small models to guide a larger language model toward preferred behavior without fine-tuning the large model. The large model remains frozen and supplies candidate text. A tuned small model and its untuned counterpart provide the guidance used to choose among those candidates.

The method performs greedy search at inference time, seeking to maximize the difference between the small models’ log probabilities. This difference captures how tuning changes their preferences. Experiments use tuned and untuned GPT-2 models for sentiment-controlled generation and summarization, demonstrating alignment improvements without additional training of the large model.

On AlpacaEval 2.0, off-the-shelf small models also improve instruction following for both white-box and black-box large models. Length-controlled win rates against GPT-4-turbo rise from 34.4% to 37.9% for Llama-3-70B-Instruct and from 16.0% to 20.1% for GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct. The guiding models themselves achieve roughly 10%. These results show that useful preference guidance can transfer from a weaker model even when its standalone answers are less competitive.
neurips-2024-weak-to-strong-search-align.tldr: Small tuned and untuned models guide test-time search to improve a frozen larger model’s alignment.

paragraphs: This paper examines how regularization affects neural-network layers whose parameter matrices multiply together. Attention contains such products in its key-query and value-projection transformations. The authors investigate why applying weight decay or L2 regularization to the individual matrices can encourage their products to become low rank.

For the studied factorized objective, the authors connect local minima of L2-regularized training to minima of a nuclear-norm-regularized objective on the matrix product. Nuclear-norm regularization provides the link to low-rank structure. They also show that the two losses become identical exponentially quickly during training, explaining why the effect can emerge early rather than only at convergence.

Empirical results confirm substantial rank reductions in attention matrix products under weight decay, including fully online training. The authors find that inducing low rank in these products can hurt language-model performance. They also observe benefits from treating attention-layer weight decay separately from decay on other parameters. The findings show that a common regularizer can alter attention’s effective matrix structure in ways that matter for performance.
neurips-2024-weight-decay-induces-low-ra.tldr: Weight decay can reduce the rank of attention matrix products, an effect that can harm language-model performance.
